arXiv:1812.04440v2 [math.AP] 09 Apr 2019

Spreading properties of a three-component reaction-diffusion model for the population of farmers and hunter-gatherers

Dongyuan Xiao    Ryunosuke Mori
February 26 2019
Abstract

In this paper, we investigate the spreading properties of solutions of farmer and hunter-gatherer model which is a three-component reaction-diffusion system. Ecologically, the model describes the geographical spreading of an initially localized population of farmers into a region occupied by hunter-gatherers. This model was proposed by Aoki, Shida and Shigesada in 1996. By numerical simulations and some formal linearization arguments, they concluded that there are four different types of spreading behaviors depending on the parameter values. Despite such intriguing observations, no mathematically rigorous studies have been made to justify their claims. The main difficulty comes from the fact that the comparison principle does not hold for the entire system. In this paper, we give theoretical justification to all of the four types of spreading behaviors observed by Aoki et al.. Furthermore, we show that a logarithmic phase drift of the front position occurs as in the scalar KPP equation. We also investigate the case where the motility of the hunter-gatherers is larger than that of the farmers, which is not discussed in the paper of Aoki et al..

Key words: Farmer and hunter-gatherer model; long time behavior; spreading speed;  logarithmic correction

1 Introduction

Early in the stone age, our ancestors lived as hunter-gatherers, which means, instead of growing their food, they lived on hunting, fishing and gathering berries and eggs of birds in the forest. As humans evolved, agriculture gradually appeared independently in different parts of the globe. At least 11 separate regions of the Old and New World were identified as independent centers of the origin of agriculture. Tracing the origins of early farming and its spreading has been the major subject of interest for a long time. For instance, the study of the origins of farming in the Near East and its dispersal to Europe has been done by many archaeologists, anthropologists, linguists, and geneticists. Many archaeological evidences certified that agriculture emerged about 11,000 years ago in the Near East before reaching North Europe about 5,000 years later. Furthermore, genetic studies tended to support that farmers in the North Europe have noticeable genetic affinity to Near East populations. It suggests that agriculture did not only spread solely across Europe as a cultural process, but also in concert with a migration of people. This fact motivated ecologists to model this kind of geographical spreading of an initially localized farmers into a region occupied by hunters and gatherers as a reaction-diffusion process in an infinite habitat.

In 1996, Aoki, Shida and Shigesada [1] proposed the following three-component reaction-diffusion system to study the process of Neolithic transition from hunter-gatherers to farmers (actually, in [1], they only considered the case N=1N=1, but in the present paper we formulate the problem in a general space dimension N≥1N\geq 1):

{∂tF=D​Δ​F+rf​F​(1−(F+C)/K),∂tC=D​Δ​C+rc​C​(1−(F+C)/K)+e⁡(F+C)​H,in​ℝN,∂tH=Dh​Δ​H+rh​H​(1−H/L)−e⁡(F+C)​H.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}F=D\Delta F+r_{f}F(1-(F+C)/K),\\ &\partial_{t}C=D\Delta C+r_{c}C(1-(F+C)/K)+e(F+C)H,\ \ \ \ \ \ \mbox{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{N},\\ &\partial_{t}H=D_{h}\Delta H+r_{h}H(1-H/L)-e(F+C)H.\end{aligned}\right.

The population densities of initial farmers, converted farmers and hunter-gatherers are represented by FF, CC and HH, respectively. This model contains seven positive parameters: DhD_{h} is the diffusion coefficient of hunter-gatherers, which is assumed to be greater than or equal to the diffusion coefficient D>0D>0 of farmers; rfr_{f}, rcr_{c} and rhr_{h} are the intrinsic growth rates; KK and LL are the carrying capacities of farmers and hunter-gatherers; ee is the conversion rate of hunter-gatherers to farmers. Note that, in [1], DhD_{h} is always assumed to be equal to DD. However, we do not see any reason to assume that the hunter-gatherers diffuse at the same speed as the farmers. It may be more natural to imagine that the hunter-gatherers would diffuse faster than the hunters. For this reason, in the present paper, we assume Dh≥DD_{h}\geq D rather than Dh=DD_{h}=D. As we will see later, the case Dh>DD_{h}>D is much harder to analyze than the case Dh=DD_{h}=D.

As shown in [1], by a suitable change of variables, the above system is converted to:

{∂tF=Δ​F+a​F​(1−F−C),∂tC=Δ​C+C⁡(1−F−C)+s​H​(F+C),in​ℝN,∂tH=d​Δ​H+b​H​(1−H−g⁡(F+C)),\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}F=\Delta F+aF(1-F-C),\\ &\partial_{t}C=\Delta C+C(1-F-C)+sH(F+C),\ \ \ \ \ \ \mbox{in}\ \mathbb{R}^{N},\\ &\partial_{t}H=d\Delta H+bH(1-H-g(F+C)),\end{aligned}\right. (1.1)

where d=Dh/D≥1d=D_{h}/D\geq 1, a=rf/rca=r_{f}/r_{c}, b=rh/rcb=r_{h}/r_{c}, s=e​L/rcs=eL/r_{c} and g=e​K/rhg=eK/r_{h}. We consider the following initial condition

H(0,x)≡1,C(0,x)≡0,F(0,x)=F0(x)≥0(F0≢0),H(0,x)\equiv 1,\ \ C(0,x)\equiv 0,\ \ F(0,x)=F_{0}(x)\geq 0\ \ (F_{0}\not\equiv 0), (1.2)

where F0​(x)F_{0}(x) is a compactly supported continuous function. The reason why we consider such initial data is because our goal is to understand how agriculture spread over a region that was originally occupied by hunter-gatherers. Thus our problem is to analyze the "spreading fronts" of the farmer populations that start from localized initial data.

In the special case a=1a=1, by setting G=F+CG=F+C, the total population density of all farmers, the system (1.1) reduces to the two-component system of predator-prey type:

{∂tG=Δ​G+G⁡(1+s​H−G),∂tH=d​Δ​H+b​H​(1−H−g​G).\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}G=\Delta G+G(1+sH-G),\\ &\partial_{t}H=d\Delta H+bH(1-H-gG).\end{aligned}\right. (1.3)

The long time behavior of the system (1.3) (with a=1a=1) has been studied by Hilhost, Mimura and Weidenfel in [12]. Among other things they proved that the solution converges to a spatially constant steady state as t→∞t\rightarrow\infty. They also considered the case where the coefficients ss, gg are replaced by s/εs/\varepsilon, g/εg/\varepsilon and studied the limit of the solution as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0. However, how fast the front propagates to infinity was not discussed in [12]. The first result on the spreading speeds for predator-prey systems was obtained by Ducrot, Giletti and Matano in [7], where they treated two-species predator-prey system that are different from (1.3).

In the general case a≠1a\neq 1, the ODE system corresponding to (1.1) possesses the following four different types of steady states:

(F,C,H)={(0,0,0),(0,0,1),(F^,C^,0),whereF^+C^=1,F^,C^≥0,(0,C∗,H∗),whereC∗=(1+s)/(1+sg),H∗=(1−g)/(1+sg)).(F,C,H)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &(0,0,0),\ (0,0,1),\\ &(\widehat{F},\widehat{C},0),\ \ \mbox{where}\ \ \widehat{F}+\widehat{C}=1,\ \widehat{F},\widehat{C}\geq 0,\\ &(0,C^{*},H^{*}),\ \ \mbox{where}\ \ C^{*}=(1+s)/(1+sg),\ H^{*}=(1-g)/(1+sg)).\end{aligned}\right.

The first two steady states always exist and unstable. The third one is a line of neutral equilibria, which always exists and stable if g≥1g\geq 1. The fourth one exists and is stable if and only if g<1g<1. It implies that there exist different expanding patterns which is determined by the value of gg. Let us remark that g=e​K/rhg=eK/r_{h}, which means the value of gg highly depends on the value of the conversion rate ee. Note that, throughout this paper, we call the case g≥1g\geq 1 by high conversion rate case and the case g<1g<1 by low conversion rate case. Ecologically speaking, if the conversion rate is sufficiently high, hunter-gatherers will completely convert into farmers, whereas hunter-gatherers and farmers can coexist if the conversion rate is low enough.

1.1 Observations by Aoki et al.

In the above mentioned paper [1], the authors observed four different types of spreading behaviors depending on the parameter values, namely those of aa, ss and gg in the system (1.1). Their observation of the spreading fronts was done by numerical simulations. Strictly speaking, they did not consider truly localized initial data for the farmers, but they set C0≡0C_{0}\equiv 0 and chose F0F_{0} to be a Heaviside function: F0=1​(x≤0)F_{0}=1\ (x\leq 0), F0​(x)=0​(x>0)F_{0}(x)=0\ (x>0). In order to estimate the speed of the spreading fronts, they again relied mainly on numerical simulations, but also calculated by formal analysis of the minimal speed of the traveling wave (comprising of the advancing front of the farmers and the retreating front of the hunter-gatherers) and confirmed that the numerically observed spreading speed well agreed with the formally calculated minimal traveling wave speed. The following figures illustrate the shape of what they call the transient waveforms.

In order to make our motivation clearer, we give a brief explanation of what was observed by Aoki et al. [1] before stating our main results. As mentioned above, their observation was done by numerical simulation combined with a formal analysis of the minimal speed of traveling wave.

  • •

    The spreading speed of the solution of the system (1.1) is always determined by max⁡{2​a,2​1+s}\max\{2\sqrt{a},2\sqrt{1+s}\}.

  • •

    The behaviors of solutions on the leading edge where the hunter-gatherers have little contact with the farmers are almost the same between the high conversion rate case and the low conversion rate case (see Figure 1-4, Leading edge).

  • •

    In the case where a<1+sa<1+s, a wave of advance of initial farmers FF is not generated (see Figure 2 and Figure 4). If, in addition that g<1g<1, the initial farmers FF disappear entirely (see Figure 4). Whereas, if g≥1g\geq 1, behind the wavefront, farmers have almost reached carrying capacity and hunter-gatherers have just about disappeared (see Figure 2, Final zone).

  • •

    In the case where a>1+sa>1+s, an advancing wavefront of initial farmers FF is also generated (see Figure 1 and Figure 3). If, in addition that g<1g<1, the waveform is a small peak with leading edge and trailing edge that converge to 00 (see Figure 3).

The goal of the present paper is to give rigorous justification to all of the above observations, and also to discuss the case where d>1d>1 that has not been treated in [1]. The case d>1d>1, turns out to be much harder to analyze. Further, we also prove logarithmic drift of the fronts for some cases.

1.2 Outline of the paper

We will present our main results in Section 2. Some results are stated for the special case d=1d=1 (Theorems 2.4 and 2.8 and part of Theorems 2.10 and 2.12), which is the case that was treated in [1]. Other results are stated for d≥1d\geq 1.The proof of the main results will be carried out in the subsequent sections.

In Section 3, we prove Theorem 2.3 which is concerned with the behaviors at the leading edge that appears in all of Figure 1-4. Since there is little interaction between the farmers and the hunter-gatherers on the leading edge, the analysis of this zone is rather straightforward.

In Section 4, we prove Theorem 2.12 on the logarithmic phase drift of the front. The logarithmic phase drift for the scalar KPP equation was studied in detail by Bramson [3, 4] by using a probabilistic method. More recently, a much simpler PDE proof has been proposed by Hamel, Nolen, Requejoffre and Ryzhik [13]. Their method is based on a super and sub-solution argument. Our proof of Theorem 2.12 is also based on a super and sub-solution argument, but the sub-solution is quite different from that in [13] since their sub-solution does not work for systems of equations.

In Section 5, we prove Theorems 2.4 and 2.5 that are concerned with the uniform positivity of solution in the final zone. Theorem 2.4 is concerned with the case 1+s≥a1+s\geq a (which corresponds to Figure 2 and 4 above), while Theorem 2.5 is concerned with the case 1+s<a1+s<a (which corresponds to Figure 1 and 3 above). Intriguingly, the proof of the two theorem are quite different: the proof of Theorem 2.4 uses a limit argument that was employed in [7] to show "pointwise spreading". The proof of Theorem 2.5 uses the result on the logarithmic drift stated in Theorem 2.12.

In Section 6, we will study final asymptotic profiles of solutions in the final zone and complete the proof of Theorems 2.8, 2.9 and 2.10, thus comfirming the profiles shown in Figure 1-4. The proof is based on the conclusion of the results in Theorems 2.4 and 2.5, and a certain limit argument.

Finally in the appendix, we give the proof of Proposition 4.1 which plays an important role in the proof of Theorem 2.12 in Section 4

2 Main results

Front propagation for scalar reaction-diffusion equations has been studied extensively and there is vast literature on this theme. Early in 1937, Fisher [9] and Kolmogorov, Petrovsky and Piskunov [11] introduced a scalar reaction-diffusion equation with monostable nonlinearity as a model equation in population genetics, which studies the propagation of dominant gene in homogeneous environment. In particular, [11] made an important early analysis of the structure of the set of traveling waves for a special class of monostable reaction-diffusion equation, the so-called KPP equation. Application of reaction-diffusion equations to ecology was pioneered by Skellam [14] in 1951. As regards the propagation of fronts for solutions with compactly supported initial data (that is, the so-called “spreading front”) is concerned, the first rigorous mathematical results in multi-dimensional homogeneous environment were provided by Aronson and Weinberger [2], for the case of monostable nonlinearity and also for bistable nonlinearity. The paper [2] introduced the notion of what we now call “spreading speed”, the meaning of which is specified Remark 2.2 below. However, apart from some recent works such as [7], much less is known about the spreading properties for systems of equations for which the comparison principle does not hold.

Note that the nonlinear terms of the first two equations in the system (1.1) are similar to the well-known KPP nonlinearity if we neglect the term HH. Hence, we first recall the classical spreading result for the monostable scalar equation from Aronson and Weinberger [2]:

Proposition 2.1 (Spreading for the scalar KPP equation ([2]))

Consider the so-called KPP equation

∂tu⁡(t,x)=d​Δ​u​(t,x)+u​f​(u⁡(t,x)),t>0,x∈ℝN,\partial_{t}u(t,x)=d\Delta u(t,x)+uf(u(t,x)),\ t>0,\ x\in\mathbb{R}^{N}, (2.1)

wherein f∈C1​(ℝ)f\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}) satisfies

f(1)=0,f(u)>0andf(u)≤f(0)for allu∈[0,1).f(1)=0,\ f(u)>0\ \ \mbox{and}\ \ f(u)\leq f(0)\ \ \mbox{for all}\ \ u\in[0,1).

Define c∗​(d,f)=2​d​f​(0)c^{*}(d,f)=2\sqrt{df(0)}. Then, for any nontrivial compactly supported and continuous function u0​(x)u_{0}(x), the solution u≡u⁡(t,x,u0​(x))u\equiv u(t,x;u_{0}(x)) of (2.1) with the initial data u0​(x)u_{0}(x) satisfies:

limt→+∞​sup∥x∥≤c​t​|1−u⁡(t,x)|=0, 0<c<c∗​(d,f),\underset{t\to+\infty}{\lim}\underset{\lVert x\rVert\leq ct}{\sup}|1-u(t,x)|=0,\ 0<c<c^{*}(d,f),

and

limt→+∞​sup∥x∥≥c​t​u​(t,x)=0,c>c∗​(d,f).\underset{t\to+\infty}{\lim}\underset{\lVert x\rVert\geq ct}{\sup}u(t,x)=0,\ c>c^{*}(d,f).

Moreover, the quantity c∗​(d,f)c^{*}(d,f) coincides with the minimal speed of traveling wave solutions of the equation (2.1) connecting 00 to 11.

Remark 2.2

Usually the term “spreading front” regards to a front of a solution that propagates to infinity from localized initial data, typically those that are compactly supported. The term “spreading speed” refers to a quantity c∗c^{*} for which the last two estimates of Proposition 2.1 hold. Thus the distance between the sphere of radius c∗​tc^{*}t and the actual position of the front is of order o⁡(t)o(t).

2.1 Uniform spreading properties

In this subsection, we present our main results on the spreading properties of solutions of the system (1.1). Throughout this paper, we define the two quantities c∗c^{*} and c∗⁣∗c^{**} as c∗:=max⁡{2​a,2​1+s}c^{*}:=\max\{2\sqrt{a},2\sqrt{1+s}\} and c∗⁣∗:=min⁡{2​a,2​1+s}c^{**}:=\min\{2\sqrt{a},2\sqrt{1+s}\}. Our first result is about the analysis of the leading edge, which provides an upper estimate on the spreading speed. As we observed from Figure 11-44, for all four cases, the behaviors of solutions are almost same on the leading edge. The first three theorems hold regardless of the size of the conversion rate.

Theorem 2.3

For any given c>c∗c>c^{*}, the solution (F,C,H)(F,C,H) of the system (1.1) with the initial data (1.2) satisfies:

limt→∞sup∥x∥≥c​t(∣1−H⁡(t,x)∣+F⁡(t,x)+C⁡(t,x))=0.\lim_{t\to\infty}\sup_{\lVert x\rVert\geq ct}\Big(\mid 1-H(t,x)\mid+F(t,x)+C(t,x)\Big)=0. (2.2)

The most difficult part of the analysis is the behaviors of the solutions in the final zone, where original hunter-gatherers, initial farmers and converted farmers heavily interact with each other. A large part of the present thesis is devoted to the analysis in this final zone. Our third result deals with the propagation of farmers in the final zone, which provides an lower estimate on the spreading speed. As we observed from Figure 11-44, for all four cases, the spreading speed is determined by the larger value of 2​1+s2\sqrt{1+s} and 2​a2\sqrt{a}.

If d=1d=1 and 1+s≥a1+s\geq a, then for any given 0≤c<c∗0\leq c<c^{*}, there exists ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that the solution (F,C,H)(F,C,H) of the system (1.1) with the initial data (1.2) satisfies:

lim inft→∞​inf∥x∥≤c​t​(F+C)​(t,x)≥ε,\underset{t\to\infty}{\liminf}\underset{\lVert x\rVert\leq ct}{\inf}(F+C)(t,x)\geq\varepsilon, (2.3)

If 1+s<a1+s<a, then for any given 0≤c<c∗0\leq c<c^{*}, there exists ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that the solution (F,C,H)(F,C,H) of the system (1.1) with the initial data (1.2) satisfies:

lim inft→∞​inf∥x∥≤c​t​(F+C)​(t,x)≥ε,\underset{t\to\infty}{\liminf}\underset{\lVert x\rVert\leq ct}{\inf}(F+C)(t,x)\geq\varepsilon, (2.5)

In present paper, we use two different approaches to prove the results of Theorem 2.4 and Theorem 2.5, respectively. We specially note that the result of Theorem 2.4 could be extended to the general case d≥1d\geq 1 by applying a similar argument to that in section 5, and the details will be provided in our future work.

Remark 2.7

The results of Theorem 2.3, Theorem 2.4 and Theorem 2.5 can be regarded as an analogue of the well-known "hair-trigger effect" for scalar monostable equation [2]. Moreover, one may find that the spreading speed of the system is always equal to c∗c^{*}, which is only determined by the parameters in the FF-equation and CC-equation. This is due to the initial data H0​(x)≡1H_{0}(x)\equiv 1, which means hunter-gatherers have already spread to the whole region.

At last, we show our main results about the asymptotic profiles of solutions in the final zone. For the high conversion rate case, Theorem 2.8 and Theorem 2.9 imply that all of the original hunter-gatherers convert to farmers at last. However, the explicit profiles of the FF-component and CC-component in the final zone are yet to be investigated. Nevertheless, for the low conversion rate case, we will show that the FF-component always converges to 00 in the final zone. In order to do this, one need first prove that the population density of hunter-gatherers would stay positive uniformly. From some ecological observations, this may happen if the conversion rate is small enough or the product of the intrinsic growth rate and the diffusion speed of hunter-gatherers is large enough. Then, we can investigate how the CC-component and HH-component behave in the finial zone by considering the dynamics of the underlying ODE system:

{Ct=C⁡(1−C)+s​C​H,Ht=b​H​(1−H−g​C).\left\{\begin{aligned} &C_{t}=C(1-C)+sCH,\\ &H_{t}=bH(1-H-gC).\end{aligned}\right. (2.12)

We expect the solution of the PDE system (1.1) to converge uniformly to the equilibrium (C∗,H∗)(C^{*},H^{*}) in the final zone as t→+∞t\to+\infty. We prove the conjecture by the established fact that a strict Lyapunov function exists. Note that, the ODE system (2.12) is a well-known Lotka-Volterra system with logistic growth rate. In population dynamics, especially prey-predator systems, ODE models always admit a strict Lyapunov function. The concrete example will be given in the later section.

Note that, if we assume b≤1b\leq 1 as in [1] for the ecological motivation that the intrinsic growth rate of hunter-gatherers is supposed to be smaller than or equal to that of converted farmers, then for the first statement in Theorem 2.10, the condition b​d≥c∗/(1−g)bd\geq c^{*}/(1-g) could hold for large enough dd.

2.2 Logarithmic correction

Recall that, in Figure 3 and Figure 4, the behaviors of the FF-component are sightly different on the wavefront. In Figure 4, it is described by Corollary 3.2 that the distribution of initial farmers converges to 00 everywhere. However, in Figure 3, the distribution of initial farmers is peaked with leading and trailing edges converging to 00. The results stated in Theorem 2.4 and Theorem 2.5 can not explain why a small peak may occur on the wavefront. More precisely, the spreading speed being equal to c∗c^{*} does not mean that the front propagates parallel to the traveling wave of speed c∗c^{*}. Even for the scalar KPP equation, this does not hold true. Therefore, we are motivated to consider the behaviors of solutions in the area enough close to c∗​tc^{*}t.

A famous result of Bramson in [3, 4] showed that for the scalar KPP equation, there is a backward phase drift of order O⁡(log⁡t)O(\log t) from the position c∗​(f)​tc^{*}(f)t. More precisely, Bramson gave a sharp asymptotics of the location of the level sets of the solution u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) of the scalar KPP equation by using some probabilistic arguments. Let Em​(t)E_{m}(t) be the set of points in (0,+∞)(0,+\infty) where u⁡(t,⋅)=mu(t,\cdot)=m and m∈(0,1)m\in(0,1). Then, there exists a constant BB and a shift xmx_{m} depending on mm and the initial data u0u_{0} such that

Em​(t)⊂[c∗​(f)​t−32​λ∗​ln⁡t−xm−Bt,c∗​(f)​t−32​λ∗​ln⁡t−xm+Bt]fortlarge enough,E_{m}(t)\subset[c^{*}(f)t-\frac{3}{2\lambda^{*}}\ln t-x_{m}-\frac{B}{t},c^{*}(f)t-\frac{3}{2\lambda^{*}}\ln t-x_{m}+\frac{B}{t}]\ \ \mbox{for}\ \ t\ \ \mbox{large enough},

with λ∗=c∗​(f)/2\lambda^{*}=c^{*}(f)/2. Recently, this result has been explained in simple PDE terms by Hamel et al. [13]. They showed that, for every m∈(0,1)m\in(0,1) there exists B>0B>0 such that

Em​(t)⊂[c∗​(f)​t−32​λ∗​ln⁡t−B,c∗​(f)​t−32​λ∗​ln⁡t+B]fortlarge enough.E_{m}(t)\subset[c^{*}(f)t-\frac{3}{2\lambda^{*}}\ln t-B,c^{*}(f)t-\frac{3}{2\lambda^{*}}\ln t+B]\ \ \mbox{for}\ \ t\ \ \mbox{large enough}.

Moreover, Ducrot [6] extended this proposition to the multi-dimensional case by showing that there is a logarithmic backward phase drift.

For the system (1.1), the estimate of the upper bound for the level set is rather straightforward. However, in the final zone, since three components heavily interact with each other, it is hard to estimate the level set of the FF-component or CC-component separately. Hence, we just provide a slightly weak result in the present paper. The estimate of the low bound for the level set is yet to investigated. Our precise result reads as:

Theorem 2.12

For any R>0R>0, for the solution (F,C,H)(F,C,H) of the system (1.1) with the initial data (1.2), it holds:

lim inft→+∞​infx∈BR,e∈SN−1(F+C)​(t,x+(c∗​t−(N+2)​c∗min⁡{1,a}​ln⁡t)​e)>0ifa>1+s,\underset{t\to+\infty}{\liminf}\inf_{x\in B_{R},e\in S^{N-1}}\ (F+C)\Big(t,x+\Big(c^{*}t-\frac{(N+2)c^{*}}{\min\{1,a\}}\ln t\Big)e\Big)>0\ \ \mbox{if}\ \ a>1+s, (2.17)
lim supt→+∞​supx∈BR,e∈SN−1H⁡(t,x+(c∗​t−(N+2)​c∗min⁡{1,a}​ln⁡t)​e)​<1ifa>​1+s.\underset{t\to+\infty}{\limsup}\sup_{x\in B_{R},e\in S^{N-1}}\ H\Big(t,x+\Big(c^{*}t-\frac{(N+2)c^{*}}{\min\{1,a\}}\ln t\Big)e\Big)<1\ \ \mbox{if}\ \ a>1+s. (2.18)

Moreover, if d=1d=1, it holds:

lim inft→+∞​infx∈BR,e∈SN−1C⁡(t,x+(c∗​t−N+2c∗​ln⁡t)​e)>0ifa<1+s,\underset{t\to+\infty}{\liminf}\inf_{x\in B_{R},e\in S^{N-1}}\ C\Big(t,x+\Big(c^{*}t-\frac{N+2}{c^{*}}\ln t\Big)e\Big)>0\ \ \mbox{if}\ \ a<1+s, (2.19)
lim supt→+∞​supx∈BR,e∈SN−1H⁡(t,x+(c∗​t−N+2c∗​ln⁡t)​e)<1ifa<1+s,\underset{t\to+\infty}{\limsup}\sup_{x\in B_{R},e\in S^{N-1}}\ H\Big(t,x+\Big(c^{*}t-\frac{N+2}{c^{*}}\ln t\Big)e\Big)<1\ \ \mbox{if}\ \ a<1+s, (2.20)
lim inft→+∞​infx∈BR,e∈SN−1H⁡(t,x+(c∗​t−N+2c∗​ln⁡t)​e)>0ifa≠1+s.\underset{t\to+\infty}{\liminf}\inf_{x\in B_{R},e\in S^{N-1}}\ H\Big(t,x+\Big(c^{*}t-\frac{N+2}{c^{*}}\ln t\Big)e\Big)>0\ \ \mbox{if}\ \ a\neq 1+s. (2.21)

Furthermore, for the special case a=1+sa=1+s and d=1d=1, it holds:

lim inft→+∞​infx∈BR,e∈SN−1(F+C)​(t,x+(c∗​t−N+2c∗​ln⁡t)​e)>0,\underset{t\to+\infty}{\liminf}\inf_{x\in B_{R},e\in S^{N-1}}\ (F+C)\Big(t,x+\Big(c^{*}t-\frac{N+2}{c^{*}}\ln t\Big)e\Big)>0, (2.22)
lim supt→+∞​supx∈BR,e∈SN−1H⁡(t,x+(c∗​t−N+2c∗​ln⁡t)​e)<1,\underset{t\to+\infty}{\limsup}\sup_{x\in B_{R},e\in S^{N-1}}\ H\Big(t,x+\Big(c^{*}t-\frac{N+2}{c^{*}}\ln t\Big)e\Big)<1, (2.23)
lim inft→+∞​infx∈BR,e∈SN−1H⁡(t,x+(c∗​t−Nc∗​ln⁡t)​e)>0.\underset{t\to+\infty}{\liminf}\inf_{x\in B_{R},e\in S^{N-1}}\ H\Big(t,x+\Big(c^{*}t-\frac{N}{c^{*}}\ln t\Big)e\Big)>0. (2.24)
Proposition 2.13

If a>1+sa>1+s, then for the solution (F,C,H)(F,C,H) of the system (1.1) with initial data (1.2), for any c<c∗c<c^{*}, it holds:

lim supt→∞sup∥x∥≥c​tF⁡(t,x)>0.\limsup_{t\rightarrow\infty}\sup_{\lVert x\rVert\geq ct}F(t,x)>0. (2.25)
Remark 2.14

By combining with Theorem 2.3 and Theorem 2.10, Proposition 2.13 explains the reason why a small peak of initial farmers can be observed on the wavefront just in the case a>1+sa>1+s and g<1g<1.

3 Upper estimates on the spreading speeds

In this section, we deal with the spreading properties of solutions of the system (1.1) on the leading edge and complete the proof of Theorem 2.3. Since there is no interaction between farmers and hunter-gatherers on the leading edge, the analysis of this zone is rather straightforward. We first prove that the initial farmers FF and converted farmers CC cannot propagate faster than the speed c∗c^{*}. Hence, on the leading edge, the contact between farmers and hunter-gatherers will never happen. Therefore, the population density of hunter-gatherers remain unchanged in this zone. This follows from a simple comparison argument.

We first concern with the analysis of the FF-component and CC-component on the leading edge and begin the proof with some simple upper estimates on the spreading speed. Note that, the nonlinear term a​F​(1−C−F)aF(1-C-F) in the FF-equation is nonincreasing on the value of CC, and the CC-component is always nonnegative. Since c∗≥2​ac^{*}\geq 2\sqrt{a}, for all e∈SN−1e\in S^{N-1}, one can construct a well-known super-solution F\cc@style​¯e:=A1e−c∗(x⋅e−c∗t)/2\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{F}_{e}:=A_{1}e^{-c^{*}(x\cdot e-c^{*}t)/2} of the equation

∂tF=Δ​F+a​F​(1−F).\partial_{t}F=\Delta F+aF(1-F).

Applying the comparison principle, one has

for allc>c∗,limt→+∞​sup∥x∥≥c​t​F​(t,x)≤limt→+∞​sup∥x∥≥c​tinfe∈SN−1​F\cc@style​¯e​(t,x)=0,\mbox{for all}\ \ c>c^{*},\ \ \underset{t\to+\infty}{\lim}\underset{\lVert x\rVert\geq ct}{\sup}F(t,x)\leq\underset{t\to+\infty}{\lim}\underset{\lVert x\rVert\geq ct}{\sup}\ \ \underset{e\in S^{N-1}}{\inf}\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{F}_{e}(t,x)=0, (3.1)

provided that A1A_{1} is large enough such that F\cc@style​¯e​(0,x)≥F⁡(0,x)\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{F}_{e}(0,x)\geq F(0,x).

Remark 3.1

Even if 1+s>a1+s>a, one may find that the function F\cc@style​¯e∗=A∗​e−a​(x⋅e−2​a​t)\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{F}^{*}_{e}=A^{*}e^{-\sqrt{a}(x\cdot e-2\sqrt{a}t)} is always a super-solution of the FF-component, provided that A∗A^{*} is large enough. It implies that , if 1+s>a1+s>a, then for any c>2​ac>2\sqrt{a}, it holds:

lim supt→+∞sup∥x∥≥ctF(t,x)=0.\limsup_{t\to+\infty}\sup_{\lVert x\lVert\geq ct}\ F(t,x)=0.

Moreover, concluding from Theorem 2.10 and Remark 3.1, the following corollary is an immediate result.

Corollary 3.2

If g<1g<1 and a<1+sa<1+s, then the solution of the system (1.1) with the initial data (1.2) satisfies:

lim supt→∞​supx∈ℝN​F​(t,x)=0,\underset{t\to\infty}{\limsup}\underset{x\in\mathbb{R}^{N}}{\sup}F(t,x)=0, (3.2)

provided that

g<min⁡{1,a}min⁡{1,a}+sord​b≥c∗1−g.g<\frac{\min\{1,a\}}{\min\{1,a\}+s}\ \ \mbox{or}\ \ db\geq\frac{c^{*}}{1-g}.

To get the estimate of the CC-component, we need to construct another suitable super-solution. Note that the nonlinear term C⁡(1−C−F)+s⁡(C+F)​HC(1-C-F)+s(C+F)H in the CC-equation is neither monotone increasing nor decreasing with respect to the value of FF. Hence, to construct a super-solution for the CC-component, it is necessary to control the value of FF suitably. However, thanks to the fact that the FF-component is sufficient small on the leading edge, one just need to deal with the following equation

∂tC=Δ​C+C⁡(1−C)+s⁡(C+F\cc@style​¯e).\partial_{t}C=\Delta C+C(1-C)+s(C+\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{F}_{e}). (3.3)

Then, we introduce the new function

C\cc@style​¯e:=A2​e−λ⁡(x⋅e−c​t)for allc>c∗,e∈SN−1.\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{C}_{e}:=A_{2}e^{-\lambda(x\cdot e-ct)}\ \ \mbox{for all}\ \ c>c^{*},\ e\in S^{N-1}.

One may find that, for large enough A2>0A_{2}>0, there exists λ=c∗/2\lambda=c^{*}/2 such that C\cc@style​¯e\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{C}_{e} satisfies

∂tC\cc@style​¯e−Δ​C\cc@style​¯e−C\cc@style​¯e​(1+s−C\cc@style​¯e)−s​F\cc@style​¯e\displaystyle\partial_{t}\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{C}_{e}-\Delta\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{C}_{e}-\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{C}_{e}(1+s-\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{C}_{e})-s\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{F}_{e}
≥\displaystyle\geq ((cλ−λ2−1−s)A2−sA1)e−c∗/2(x⋅e−ct)\displaystyle\Big((c\lambda-\lambda^{2}-1-s)A_{2}-sA_{1}\Big)e^{-c^{*}/2(x\cdot e-ct)}
≥\displaystyle\geq 0.\displaystyle 0.

Moreover, C⁡(0,x)=0C(0,x)=0 for any x∈ℝNx\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. We can now apply the comparison principle again to conclude that

for allc′>c,limt→+∞​sup∥x∥≥c′​t​C​(t,x)≤limt→+∞​sup∥x∥≥c′​t​infe∈SN−1​C\cc@style​¯e​(t,x)=0.\mbox{for all}\ \ c^{\prime}>c,\ \ \underset{t\to+\infty}{\lim}\underset{\lVert x\rVert\geq c^{\prime}t}{\sup}C(t,x)\leq\underset{t\to+\infty}{\lim}\underset{\lVert x\rVert\geq c^{\prime}t}{\sup}\ \underset{e\in S^{N-1}}{\inf}\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{C}_{e}(t,x)=0. (3.4)

For the reason that cc can be chosen arbitrarily close to c∗c^{*}, one can conclude that the CC-component does not spread faster that the spreading speed c∗c^{*}.

To complete this section , we deal with the upper estimate of the HH-component on leading edge. One may find that the HH-component is always able to stay positive outside of the farmer’s range. The main idea is to construct a suitable sub-solution for the HH-component as follows:

H\cc@style​¯e:=1−g(A1+A2)e−c∗(x⋅e−ct)/(2d)for allc>c∗,e∈SN−1.\underaccent{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{H}_{e}:=1-g(A_{1}+A_{2})e^{-c^{*}(x\cdot e-ct)/(2d)}\ \ \mbox{for all}\ \ c>c^{*},\ e\in S^{N-1}.

{∂tH\cc@style​¯=dΔH\cc@style​¯+bH\cc@style​¯(1−g(A1+A2)e−c∗(x⋅e−ct)/2−H\cc@style​¯),H\cc@style​¯​(0,x)=1.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}\underaccent{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{H}=d\Delta\underaccent{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{H}+b\underaccent{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{H}(1-g(A_{1}+A_{2})e^{-c^{*}(x\cdot e-ct)/2}-\underaccent{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{H}),\\ &\underaccent{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{H}(0,x)=1.\end{aligned}\right. (3.5)

H\cc@style​¯​(0,x)≥H\cc@style​¯e​(0,x).\underaccent{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{H}(0,x)\geq\underaccent{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{H}_{e}(0,x).

limt→∞​inf∥x∥≥c′t​H​(t,x)≥limt→∞​inf∥x∥≥c′t​supe∈SN−1​H\cc@style​¯e​(t,x)=1for allc′>c.\underset{t\to\infty}{\lim}\underset{\lVert x\lVert\geq c^{\prime}t}{\inf}H(t,x)\geq\underset{t\to\infty}{\lim}\underset{\lVert x\lVert\geq c^{\prime}t}{\inf}\ \underset{e\in S^{N-1}}{\sup}\underaccent{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{H}_{e}(t,x)=1\ \ \mbox{for all}\ \ c^{\prime}>c.

4 Logarithmic Bramson correction

At first, we would like to introduce an important result provided in [6, 13]. Consider the linear equation with drift term as follows:

∂tz=∂ξ2z+(c∗−δt+t0+N−1ξ+ξt0δ​(t))​∂ξz+λ∗2​z,t>0,ξ>0,\partial_{t}z=\partial_{\xi}^{2}z+\Big(c^{*}-\frac{\delta}{t+t_{0}}+\frac{N-1}{\xi+\xi^{\delta}_{t_{0}}(t)}\Big)\partial_{\xi}z+\lambda^{*2}z,\ \ t>0,\ \xi>0, (4.1)

where

λ∗=c∗/2andξt0δ​(t):=c∗​(t+t0)−δ​ln⁡t+t0t0.\lambda^{*}=c^{*}/2\ \ \mbox{and}\ \ \xi^{\delta}_{t_{0}}(t):=c^{*}(t+t_{0})-\delta\ln\frac{t+t_{0}}{t_{0}}.

Then the following proposition holds:

Proposition 4.1

Let zt0δ​(ξ,t)z^{\delta}_{t_{0}}(\xi,t) be the solution of the equation (4.1) with boundary condition

zt0δ​(t,0)=0for allt>0,z^{\delta}_{t_{0}}(t,0)=0\ \ \mbox{for all}\ \ t>0,

and the initial data

zt0δ(0,ξ)=e−λ∗​ξζ0(t0−1/2ξ)≥0for allξ≥0,z^{\delta}_{t_{0}}(0,\xi)=e^{-\lambda^{*}\xi}\zeta_{0}(t_{0}^{-1/2}\xi)\geq 0\ \ \mbox{for all}\ \ \xi\geq 0,

where ζ0​(⋅)\zeta_{0}(\cdot) is an nontrivial compactly supported smooth function. Then it holds:

zt0δ​(t,ξ)=(t+t0)γ−12t0γ​ξ​e−λ∗​ξ​{∫0∞ζ0​(ρ)​ρ​𝑑ρ+h1​(t,t0)π​e−ξ24​(t+t0)+h2​(t,ξ,t0)},ξ≥0,t≥0,z^{\delta}_{t_{0}}(t,\xi)=\frac{(t+t_{0})^{\gamma-\frac{1}{2}}}{t_{0}^{\gamma}}\xi e^{-\lambda^{*}\xi}\Big\{\frac{\int_{0}^{\infty}\zeta_{0}(\rho)\rho d\rho+h_{1}(t,t_{0})}{\sqrt{\pi}}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}}{4(t+t_{0})}}+h_{2}(t,\xi,t_{0})\Big\},\ \ \xi\geq 0,\ t\geq 0, (4.2)

where γ:=δ​λ∗−N+12\gamma:=\delta\lambda^{*}-\frac{N+1}{2}, h1h_{1} and h2h_{2} are smooth functions satisfying

{|h1(t,t0)|≤B1t0−1/2∥ζ0∥m,|h2​(t,ξ,t0)|≤B2​{t01/4​∥ζ0∥m(t+t0)1/2+(t0t+t0)1−B2t0​∥∂ρ2ζ0∥m}​e−ξ28​(t+t0),ξ≥0,t≥0,\left\{\begin{aligned} &|h_{1}(t,t_{0})|\leq B_{1}t_{0}^{-1/2}\lVert\zeta_{0}\rVert_{m},\\ &|h_{2}(t,\xi,t_{0})|\leq B_{2}\Big\{\frac{t_{0}^{1/4}\lVert\zeta_{0}\rVert_{m}}{(t+t_{0})^{1/2}}+\Big(\frac{t_{0}}{t+t_{0}}\Big)^{1-\frac{B_{2}}{\sqrt{t_{0}}}}\lVert\partial_{\rho}^{2}\zeta_{0}\rVert_{m}\Big\}e^{-\frac{\xi^{2}}{8(t+t_{0})}},\end{aligned}\right.\ \ \ \ \xi\geq 0,\ t\geq 0,

for some positive constants B1B_{1} and B2B_{2}. Here, the norm ∥⋅∥m\lVert\cdot\rVert_{m} is defined as

∥ζ0∥m2:=∫0∞ζ0​(ρ)2​eρ24​𝑑ρ.\lVert\zeta_{0}\rVert_{m}^{2}:=\int_{0}^{\infty}\zeta_{0}(\rho)^{2}e^{\frac{\rho^{2}}{4}}d\rho.

Note that, this proposition is slightly different from those of [6, 13]. Hence, we will give the proof in the appendix for the sake of completeness.

Now, let us consider the solution (F,C,H)(F,C,H) of the system (1.1) with spherically symmetric initial data (F0,C0,H0)(F_{0},C_{0},H_{0}). By spatially homogeneity of the system and the uniqueness of the solution, the solution (F,C,H)(F,C,H) is also spherically symmetric. By changing the variables, the solution (F⁡(t,r),C⁡(t,r),H⁡(t,r))(F(t,r),C(t,r),H(t,r)) where r=∥x∥r=\lVert x\lVert satisfies the following one-dimensional system

{∂tF=∂r2F+N−1r​∂rF+a​F​(1−F−C),∂tC=∂r2C+N−1r​∂rC+C⁡(1−F−C)+s​H​(F+C),∂tH=d​∂r2H+d​N−1r​∂rH+b​H​(1−H−g⁡(F+C)),ξ>0,t>0.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}F=\partial_{r}^{2}F+\frac{N-1}{r}\partial_{r}F+aF(1-F-C),\\ &\partial_{t}C=\partial_{r}^{2}C+\frac{N-1}{r}\partial_{r}C+C(1-F-C)+sH(F+C),\\ &\partial_{t}H=d\partial_{r}^{2}H+d\frac{N-1}{r}\partial_{r}H+bH(1-H-g(F+C)),\end{aligned}\right.\quad\quad\xi>0,\ t>0. (4.3)

We consider the moving frame as ξ=r−ξt0​(t)\xi=r-\xi_{t_{0}}(t). Then, the functions

(ℱ⁡(t,ξ),𝒞⁡(t,ξ),ℋ⁡(t,ξ)):=(F⁡(t,ξ+ξt0​(t)),C⁡(t,ξ+ξt0​(t)),H⁡(t,ξ+ξt0​(t))CLOSE(\mathcal{F}(t,\xi),\mathcal{C}(t,\xi),\mathcal{H}(t,\xi)):=(F(t,\xi+\xi_{t_{0}}(t)),C(t,\xi+\xi_{t_{0}}(t)),H(t,\xi+\xi_{t_{0}}(t))

satisfy the system as follows:

{∂tℱ=∂ξ2ℱ+(c∗−N+22​λ∗​(t+t0)+N−1ξ+ξt0​(t))​∂ξℱ+a​ℱ​(1−ℱ−𝒞),∂t𝒞=∂ξ2𝒞+(c∗−N+22​λ∗​(t+t0)+N−1ξ+ξt0​(t))​∂ξ𝒞+𝒞⁡(1−ℱ−𝒞)+s​H​(ℱ+𝒞),∂tℋ=d​∂ξ2ℋ+d⁡(c∗−N+22​λ∗​(t+t0)+N−1ξ+ξt0​(t))​∂ξℋ+b​ℋ​(1−ℋ−g⁡(ℱ+𝒞)),ξ>−ξt0δ(t),t>0.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}\mathcal{F}=\partial_{\xi}^{2}\mathcal{F}+\Big(c^{*}-\frac{N+2}{2\lambda^{*}(t+t_{0})}+\frac{N-1}{\xi+\xi_{t_{0}}(t)}\Big)\partial_{\xi}\mathcal{F}+a\mathcal{F}(1-\mathcal{F}-\mathcal{C}),\\ &\partial_{t}\mathcal{C}=\partial_{\xi}^{2}\mathcal{C}+\Big(c^{*}-\frac{N+2}{2\lambda^{*}(t+t_{0})}+\frac{N-1}{\xi+\xi_{t_{0}}(t)}\Big)\partial_{\xi}\mathcal{C}+\mathcal{C}(1-\mathcal{F}-\mathcal{C})+sH(\mathcal{F}+\mathcal{C}),\\ &\partial_{t}\mathcal{H}=d\partial_{\xi}^{2}\mathcal{H}+d\Big(c^{*}-\frac{N+2}{2\lambda^{*}(t+t_{0})}+\frac{N-1}{\xi+\xi_{t_{0}}(t)}\Big)\partial_{\xi}\mathcal{H}+b\mathcal{H}(1-\mathcal{H}-g(\mathcal{F}+\mathcal{C})),\end{aligned}\right.\quad\quad\xi>-\xi^{\delta}_{t_{0}}(t),\ t>0.

4.1 Upper estimates on the location of the wavefront

In this subsection, we first construct suitable super-solutions for the FF-component and the CC-component, and sub-solution for the HH-component, respectively. The constructions for the cases 1+s>a1+s>a, 1+s<a1+s<a and a=1+sa=1+s are different.

We first deal with the case a>1+sa>1+s, which means the FF-component always moves faster than the CC-component. The construction for this case is rather straightforward. Let δ=δ∗:=N+22​λ∗\delta=\delta^{*}:=\frac{N+2}{2\lambda^{*}} and (u¯​(t,ξ),v¯​(t,ξ))(\bar{u}(t,\xi),\bar{v}(t,\xi)) be the solution of

{∂tu¯=∂ξ2u¯+(2​c∗−δ∗t+t0+N−1ξ+ξt0δ∗​(t))​∂ξu¯+a​u¯,∂tv¯=∂ξ2v¯+(2​c∗−δ∗t+t0+N−1ξ+ξt0δ∗​(t))​∂ξv¯+(1+s)​v¯+s​u¯,ξ>0,t>0,\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}\bar{u}=\partial^{2}_{\xi}\bar{u}+\Big(2c^{*}-\frac{\delta^{*}}{t+t_{0}}+\frac{N-1}{\xi+\xi^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t)}\Big)\partial_{\xi}\bar{u}+a\bar{u},\\ &\partial_{t}\bar{v}=\partial^{2}_{\xi}\bar{v}+\Big(2c^{*}-\frac{\delta^{*}}{t+t_{0}}+\frac{N-1}{\xi+\xi^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t)}\Big)\partial_{\xi}\bar{v}+(1+s)\bar{v}+s\bar{u},\end{aligned}\right.\quad\quad\xi>0,\ t>0,

with the boundary condition (u¯​(t,0),v¯​(t,0))=(0,0)(\bar{u}(t,0),\bar{v}(t,0))=(0,0), and with compactly supported initial data

u¯0(ξ)=a−1−ssv¯0(ξ)=e−λ∗​ξζ0(t0−1/2ξ)for allξ≥0.\bar{u}_{0}(\xi)=\frac{a-1-s}{s}\bar{v}_{0}(\xi)=e^{-\lambda^{*}\xi}\zeta_{0}(t_{0}^{-1/2}\xi)\ \ \mbox{for all}\ \ \xi\geq 0.

Then under the same notation as in Proposition 4.1, one has

(u¯​(t,ξ),v¯​(t,ξ))=(zt0δ∗​(t,ξ),sa−1−s​zt0δ∗​(t,ξ))for allξ≥0,t≥0.(\bar{u}(t,\xi),\bar{v}(t,\xi))=\Big(z^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t,\xi),\frac{s}{a-1-s}z^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t,\xi)\Big)\ \ \mbox{for all}\ \ \xi\geq 0,\ t\geq 0.

Moreover, for any μ>0\mu>0, (u¯∗​(t,x),v¯∗​(t,x)):=μ⁡(u¯​(t,∥x∥−ξt0δ∗​(t)),v¯​(t,∥x∥−ξt0δ∗​(t)))(\bar{u}^{*}(t,x),\bar{v}^{*}(t,x)):=\mu(\bar{u}(t,\lVert x\rVert-\xi^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t)),\bar{v}(t,\lVert x\rVert-\xi^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t))) satisfies

{∂tu¯∗≥Δ​u¯∗+a​u¯∗​(1−F−C),∂tv¯∗≥Δ​v¯∗+v¯∗​(1−F−C)+s​H​(u¯∗+v¯∗),ξ>ξt0δ∗(t),t>0,\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}\bar{u}^{*}\geq\Delta\bar{u}^{*}+a\bar{u}^{*}(1-F-C),\\ &\partial_{t}\bar{v}^{*}\geq\Delta\bar{v}^{*}+\bar{v}^{*}(1-F-C)+sH(\bar{u}^{*}+\bar{v}^{*}),\end{aligned}\right.\quad\quad\xi>\xi^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t),\ t>0,

where (F,C,H)(F,C,H) is the solution of the system (1.1) with the initial data (1.2).

Next, we define the functions F\cc@style​¯​(t,x)\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{F}(t,x) and C\cc@style​¯​(t,x)\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{C}(t,x) as:

F\cc@style​¯​(t,x)={B∗,∥x∥≤ξt0δ∗​(t)+A,min⁡{B∗,μ​u¯​(t,∥x∥−ξt0δ∗​(t))},∥x∥≥ξt0δ∗​(t)+A,\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{F}(t,x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcl}&B^{*},&\ \lVert x\rVert\leq\xi^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t)+A,\\ &\min\{B^{*},\mu\bar{u}(t,\lVert x\rVert-\xi^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t))\},&\ \lVert x\rVert\geq\xi^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t)+A,\end{array}\right.
C\cc@style​¯​(t,x)={1+s,∥x∥≤ξt0δ∗​(t)+A,min⁡{1+s,μ​v¯​(t,∥x∥−ξt0δ∗​(t))},∥x∥≥ξt0δ∗​(t)+A,\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{C}(t,x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcl}&1+s,&\ \lVert x\rVert\leq\xi^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t)+A,\\ &\min\{1+s,\mu\bar{v}(t,\lVert x\rVert-\xi^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t))\},&\ \lVert x\rVert\geq\xi^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t)+A,\end{array}\right.

where B∗:=sup(t,x)∈ℝ+×ℝNF⁡(t,x)B^{*}:=\sup_{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{N}}F(t,x). Furthermore, in the case of d=1d=1, we define H\cc@style​¯​(t,x)\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{H}(t,x) as

H\cc@style​¯​(t,x)={0,∥x∥≤ξt0δ∗​(t)+A,max⁡{0,1−g​μ​(u⁡(t,∥x∥−ξt0δ∗​(t))+v⁡(t,∥x∥−ξt0δ∗​(t)))},∥x∥≥ξt0δ∗​(t)+A.\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{H}(t,x)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcl}&0,&\ \lVert x\rVert\leq\xi^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t)+A,\\ &\max\{0,1-g\mu(u(t,\lVert x\rVert-\xi^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t))+v(t,\lVert x\rVert-\xi^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t)))\},&\ \lVert x\rVert\geq\xi^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t)+A.\end{array}\right.

Note that, we choose constant μ>0\mu>0 large enough such that, for all t≥0t\geq 0,

μu¯(t,A)=μzδ∗t0(t,A)>B∗,μv¯(t,A)=μ​s​zt0δ∗​(t,A)a−1−s>1+s,\displaystyle\mu\bar{u}(t,A)=\mu z^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t,A)>B^{*},\ \ \mu\bar{v}(t,A)=\frac{\mu sz^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t,A)}{a-1-s}>1+s,
μ​g​(u¯​(t,A)+v¯​(t,A))=μ​g​(a−1)a−1−s​zt0δ∗​(t,A)>1.\displaystyle\mu g(\bar{u}(t,A)+\bar{v}(t,A))=\frac{\mu g(a-1)}{a-1-s}z^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t,A)>1.

We remark that by applying Proposition 4.1, such μ>0\mu>0 always exists for sufficiently large t0>0t_{0}>0. Then by applying the comparison principle, one obtain

F(t,x)≤F\cc@style​¯(t,x),C(t,x)≤C\cc@style​¯(t,x),H(t,x)≥H\cc@style​¯(t,x)for allx∈ℝN,t>0.F(t,x)\leq\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{F}(t,x),\ C(t,x)\leq\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{C}(t,x),\ H(t,x)\geq\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{H}(t,x)\ \ \mbox{for all}\ \ x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N},\ t>0. (4.4)
Remark 4.2

Note that, for the case d>1d>1, the functions F\cc@style​¯\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{F} and C\cc@style​¯\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{C} are still super-solutions for the FF-component and the CC-component. However, the function H\cc@style​¯\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{H} could no longer be a suitable sub-solution for the HH-component.

Next, we deal with the construction for the case a=1+sa=1+s and d=1d=1. Under the same notation as in Proposition 4.1, we consider

which satisfies

{∂tu^∗=Δ​u^∗+a​u^∗,∂tv^∗=Δ​v^∗+(1+s)​v^∗+s​u^∗,ξ>ξt0δ∗(t),t>0.\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}\hat{u}^{*}=\Delta\hat{u}^{*}+a\hat{u}^{*},\\ &\partial_{t}\hat{v}^{*}=\Delta\hat{v}^{*}+(1+s)\hat{v}^{*}+s\hat{u}^{*},\end{aligned}\right.\quad\quad\xi>\xi^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t),\ t>0.

g​μ​(u^​(t,A)+v^​(t,A))=μ​g​(2+s​t)​zt0δ∗​(t,A)>1.\displaystyle g\mu(\hat{u}(t,A)+\hat{v}(t,A))=\mu g(2+st)z^{\delta^{*}}_{t_{0}}(t,A)>1.

where B∗:=sup(t,x)∈ℝ+×ℝNF⁡(t,x)B^{*}:=\sup_{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{R}^{N}}F(t,x). By applying the comparison principle, one has

, lim supt→+∞​supc∗​t−N2​λ∗​ln⁡t+r≤∥x∥​C​(t,x)→0asr→+∞.\displaystyle\underset{t\to+\infty}{\limsup}\underset{c^{*}t-\frac{N}{2\lambda^{*}}\ln t+r\leq\lVert x\rVert}{\sup}C(t,x)\to 0\ \ \mbox{as}\ \ r\to+\infty. (4.11)

lim inft→+∞​infc∗​t−N2​λ∗​ln⁡t+r≤∥x∥​H​(t,x)→1asr→+∞.\underset{t\to+\infty}{\liminf}\underset{c^{*}t-\frac{N}{2\lambda^{*}}\ln t+r\leq\lVert x\rVert}{\inf}H(t,x)\to 1\ \ \mbox{as}\ \ r\to+\infty. (4.12)

Furthermore, the following proposition which is concerned with the upper estimates of the location of the wavefront holds:

Proposition 4.5

If d=1d=1, then for the solution (F,C,H)(F,C,H) of the system (1.1) with the initial data (1.2) and for any R>0R>0, it holds:

Proof of Proposition 4.5. We first deal with the proof the statement (4.13). To proceed by contradiction, we assume that there exist r0∈ℝr_{0}\in\mathbb{R}, e∞∈SN−1e_{\infty}\in S^{N-1} and a sequence of times tn→+∞t_{n}\to+\infty such that

Up to extraction of a subsequence, the functions Hn​(t,x)=H⁡(t+tn,x+(c∗​tn−N+22​λ∗​ln⁡tn+r0)​e∞)H_{n}(t,x)=H(t+t_{n},x+(c^{*}t_{n}-\frac{N+2}{2\lambda^{*}}\ln t_{n}+r_{0})e_{\infty}) converge locally uniformly to an entire solution H∞H_{\infty} that satisfies

Since 0≤H∞≤10\leq H_{\infty}\leq 1 in ℝ×ℝ\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R} and H∞​(0,0)=0H_{\infty}(0,0)=0. The strong maximum principle implies that H∞≡0H_{\infty}\equiv 0. However, from the estimate (4.9), H∞​(0,r​e∞)≥1/2H_{\infty}(0,re_{\infty})\geq 1/2 for rr large enough. One has reached a contradiction which implies that the estimate (4.13) holds true. Since the (4.14) follows from the same argument, the proof of this proposition is thereby complete. □\square

4.2 Lower estimates on the location of the wavefront

In this subsection, we complete the proof of Theorem 2.12 by showing lower estimates for the total population F+CF+C of farmers, and the upper estimate for the HH at the position c∗​t−O⁡(ln⁡t)c^{*}t-O(\ln t). Let us first consider the case a=1+sa=1+s, which can be proved by simple comparison argument.

Proposition 4.6

Let (F,C,H)(F,C,H) be the solution of the system (1.1) with the initial data (1.2) and G⁡(t,x):=F⁡(t,x)+C⁡(t,x)G(t,x):=F(t,x)+C(t,x). If a=1+sa=1+s and d=1d=1, then for any R>0R>0, it holds:

Proof of Proposition 4.6. In the case of d=1d=1, we know that 1−max⁡{1,g}​(F+C)1-\max\{1,g\}(F+C) is a suitable sub-solution of HH, such that H≥1−max⁡{1,g}​(F+C)H\geq 1-\max\{1,g\}(F+C) for all x∈ℝNx\in\mathbb{R}^{N} and t>0t>0. Then, since a=1+sa=1+s, one has

=a​G−(a​F+C+max⁡{1,g}​s​C)​G≥(a−k​G)​G,\displaystyle=aG-(aF+C+\max\{1,g\}sC)G\geq(a-kG)G,

where k:=max⁡{a,1+max⁡{1,g}​s​C}k:=\max\{a,1+\max\{1,g\}sC\}. Then by applying the argument in [13] for scalar KPP equation and Proposition 4.1, one can complete the proof of Proposition 4.6. □\square

Next, we deal with the case a>1+sa>1+s. Note that, in this case, our estimate is not very sharp, since the coefficient c∗​(N+2)/min⁡{1,a}c^{*}(N+2)/\min\{1,a\} in front of the ln⁡t\ln t is greater than (N+2)/c∗(N+2)/c^{*} which has been proved by Bramson and Hamel et al. for the scalar KPP equation.

Proposition 4.7

Let (F,C,H)(F,C,H) be the solution of the system (1.1) with the initial data (1.2) and G⁡(t,x):=F⁡(t,x)+C⁡(t,x)G(t,x):=F(t,x)+C(t,x). If a>1+sa>1+s, then for any R>0R>0, it holds:

As a matter of fact, in the proof of Proposition 4.7, only the properties of F\cc@style​¯\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{F} and C\cc@style​¯\accentset{{\cc@style\underline{\mskip 10.0mu}}}{C} will be used.

Next, we complete the proof of Proposition 2.13 which explain the reason why FF would not uniformly converge to 00 on the wavefront in the case of a>1+sa>1+s.

Proof of Proposition 2.13. We prove by contradiction and assume that

lim supt→∞supc0​t≤∥x∥F⁡(t,x)=0for​some​c0<c∗=2​a.\limsup_{t\rightarrow\infty}\sup_{c_{0}t\leq\lVert x\rVert}F(t,x)=0\quad{\rm for\ some}\ c_{0}<c^{*}=2\sqrt{a}.

In conclusion, Theorem 2.12 is an immediate result following from Proposition 4.5, Proposition 4.7 and Proposition 4.10.

5 Lower estimates on the spreading speed

In this section, we deal with the lower estimate on the spreading speeds of solutions of the system (1.1). The proof of Theorem 2.4 and Theorem 2.5 will be performed through several subsections. Since original hunter-gatherers, initial farmers and converted farmers heavily interact with each other in the final zone, one need very delicate analysis to get uniform upper estimate of the HH-component and uniform lower estimate of the F+CF+C-component. Note that, our result only implies that the total population density of initial farmers and converted farmers is uniformly greater than 00 in the final zone as t→+∞t\to+\infty. However, we still do not how to investigate the population density of each populations of farmers separately.

Before stating our arguments, we would like to introduce some basic properties at first. Denote XX as a Banach space of ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}-valued bounded and uniformly continuous functions on ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} endowed with the usual sup-norm. Let us define Ψ⁡(r)⊂X\Psi(r)\subset X as

Ψ(r)={(ψ1,ψ2,ψ3)∈X: 0≤ψ1, 0≤ψ2,ψ1+ψ2≤rand 0≤ψ3≤1}.\Psi(r)=\{(\psi_{1},\psi_{2},\psi_{3})\in X:\ 0\leq\psi_{1},\ 0\leq\psi_{2},\ \psi_{1}+\psi_{2}\leq r\ \mbox{and}\ 0\leq\psi_{3}\leq 1\}.

Although the comparison principle does not hold for the full system, one can apply it on each equation separately. Let us denote the nonlinear semiflow generated by the system (1.1) by Z⁡(t)Z(t) and add the both sides of the FF-equation and CC-equation of the system (1.1), then one gets

∂t(F+C)−Δ⁡(F+C)=(a​F+C)​(1−F−C)+s​H​(F+C).\partial_{t}(F+C)-\Delta(F+C)=(aF+C)(1-F-C)+sH(F+C). (5.1)

Since 0≤H≤10\leq H\leq 1, the right hand side of the equation (5.1) is not greater than

min⁡{a,1}​(max⁡{a,1}+smin⁡{a,1}−F−C)​(F+C).\min\{a,1\}\Big(\frac{\max\{a,1\}+s}{\min\{a,1\}}-F-C\Big)(F+C).

By applying the comparison principle, one can conclude immediately that

supx∈ℝN(F⁡(t,x)+C⁡(t,x))≤m⁡(t),\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{N}}\Big(F(t,x)+C(t,x)\Big)\leq m(t),

where m⁡(t)m(t) is a function satisfying

d​md​t=min⁡{a,1}​(max⁡{a,1}+smin⁡{a,1}−m)​mandm⁡(0)=supx∈ℝN(F⁡(0,x)+C⁡(0,x)).\frac{dm}{dt}=\min\{a,1\}\Big(\frac{\max\{a,1\}+s}{\min\{a,1\}}-m\Big)m\ \ \mbox{and}\ \ m(0)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{N}}(F(0,x)+C(0,x)).

Therefore, if we introduce a new function as

M⁡(r):=max⁡{r,max⁡{a,1}+smin⁡{a,1}},M(r):=\max\{r,\frac{\max\{a,1\}+s}{\min\{a,1\}}\},

then one may obtain that, for each r>0r>0, it holds

Z⁡(t)​[Ψ⁡(r)]⊂Ψ⁡(M⁡(r))for allt>0.Z(t)[\Psi(r)]\subset\Psi(M(r))\ \ \mbox{for all}\ \ t>0.
Remark 5.1

If H0​(x)≡0H_{0}(x)\equiv 0, then by applying the comparison principle, one can rewrite the system (1.1) to a two-component competition system as

{∂tF=Δ​F+a​F​(1−F−C),∂tC=Δ​C+C⁡(1−F−C),\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}F=\Delta F+aF(1-F-C),\\ &\partial_{t}C=\Delta C+C(1-F-C),\end{aligned}\right.

of which the spreading properties are partly studied by Girardin and Lam in [10].

Furthermore, for the special case when the diffusion coefficient dd of the HH-equation is equal to 11, we have a direct observation as follows:

Proposition 5.2

If d=1d=1, then there exists ε∗>0\varepsilon^{*}>0 such that the solution (F,C,H)(F,C,H) of the system (1.1) satisfies:

provided that the initial data (F0,C0,H0)∈Ψ⁡(r)(F_{0},C_{0},H_{0})\in\Psi(r) satisfies F0+C0+H0≥ε∗F_{0}+C_{0}+H_{0}\geq\varepsilon^{*}.

Proof of Proposition 5.2. Let us first add the both sides of the FF-equation, CC-equation and HH-equation. One may find that, it holds

+s​H​(F+C)−g​b​H​(F+C)−b​H2\displaystyle+sH(F+C)-gbH(F+C)-bH^{2}
≥\displaystyle\geq ε2​(F+C+H)−ε3​(F+C+H)2,\displaystyle\varepsilon_{2}(F+C+H)-\varepsilon_{3}(F+C+H)^{2},

where ε2=min⁡{1,a,b}\varepsilon_{2}=\min\{1,a,b\}, ε3=max⁡{1,ε1,ε1​b}\varepsilon_{3}=\max\{1,\varepsilon_{1},\varepsilon_{1}b\} and ε1=max⁡{1,a,s,g}\varepsilon_{1}=\max\{1,a,s,g\}. Therefore, by applying the comparison principle, there exists ε∗>0\varepsilon^{*}>0 such that

inft≥0,x∈ℝN​(F+C+H)​(t,x)≥ε∗,\underset{t\geq 0,x\in\mathbb{R}^{N}}{\inf}(F+C+H)(t,x)\geq\varepsilon^{*},

provided that F0​(x)+C0​(x)+H0​(x)≥ε∗F_{0}(x)+C_{0}(x)+H_{0}(x)\geq\varepsilon^{*}. □\square

5.1 Uniform spreading in the final zone (1+s≥a1+s\geq a)

Throughout this paper, we denote c0c^{0} as an arbitrarily chosen constant speed in [0,c∗)[0,c^{*}). The proof of Theorem 2.4 is split into three steps. for each nn large enough.

5.2 Uniform spreading in the final zone (1+s<a1+s<a)

Before dealing with the proof of Theorem 2.5, we note that, by proceeding the same argument in subsection 5.1, one can obtain a lemma as follows:

Note that, one also can prove Theorem 2.4 for the case d=1d=1 by applying the same argument as above.

6 Asymptotic profiles in the final zone

In section 5, we have already shown that the propagation of farmers occurs with the speed c∗c^{*}. However, whether the profiles of solutions converges to the steady states (F^,C^,0)(\widehat{F},\widehat{C},0) or (0,C∗,H∗)(0,C^{*},H^{*}) are still unknown. In this section, we mainly deal with the asymptotic profiles of solutions in the final zone. From the numerical work of Aoki et al., we expect that the profiles of solutions in the final zone are different between the high conversion rate case and the low conversion rate case. Therefore, we split the justification of the numerical results into two parts by dealing with the cases g≥1g\geq 1 and g<1g<1, respectively.

6.1 Asymptotic profiles in the high conversion rate case (g≥1g\geq 1)

Our first result comes from a direct observation on the FF-equation of the system (1.1).

Proposition 6.1

If g≥1g\geq 1, then for any 0≤c<min⁡{2,2​a}0\leq c<\min\{2,2\sqrt{a}\}, the solution (F,C,H)(F,C,H) of the system (1.1) with the initial data (1.2) satisfies:

lim supt→∞sup∥x∥≤c​tH⁡(t,x)=0,\limsup_{t\to\infty}\sup_{\lVert x\rVert\leq ct}H(t,x)=0, (6.1)
lim supt→∞sup∥x∥≤c​t|1−(F+C)|​(t,x)=0.\limsup_{t\to\infty}\sup_{\lVert x\rVert\leq ct}|1-(F+C)|(t,x)=0. (6.2)

Proof of Proposition 6.1. Let us consider the solution G2​(t,x)G_{2}(t,x) of the following equation

{∂tG2=Δ​G2+min⁡{1,a}​G2​(1−G2),G2​(0,x)=G2,0​(x).\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}G_{2}=\Delta G_{2}+\min\{1,a\}G_{2}(1-G_{2}),\\ &G_{2}(0,x)=G_{2,0}(x).\end{aligned}\right.

Note that, G2​(t,x)≤1G_{2}(t,x)\leq 1 for all t≥0t\geq 0 and x∈ℝNx\in\mathbb{R}^{N}, provided that the initial data G2,0​(x)≤1G_{2,0}(x)\leq 1. Moreover, the function G=F+CG=F+C satisfies

∂t(F+C)\displaystyle\partial_{t}(F+C) =Δ⁡(F+C)+(a​F+C)​(1−F−C)+s​H​(F+C)\displaystyle=\Delta(F+C)+(aF+C)(1-F-C)+sH(F+C)
≥Δ​G+min⁡{1,a}​G​(1−G).\displaystyle\geq\Delta G+\min\{1,a\}G(1-G).

The last inequality holds for all (t,x)∈{(t,x)|G⁡(t,x)≤1}(t,x)\in\{(t,x)\ |\ G(t,x)\leq 1\}. Thus, by applying the comparison principle and the spreading properties of KPP equation, one can claim that:

Claim 6.2

For both cases g≥1g\geq 1 and g<1g<1, it holds:

lim inft→+∞inf∥x∥≤ct(F+C)(t,x)≥1,\liminf_{t\to+\infty}\inf_{\lVert x\lVert\leq ct}(F+C)(t,x)\geq 1, (6.3)

for all c∈[0,min⁡{2,2​a})c\in[0,\min\{2,2\sqrt{a}\}).

Now, let us choose sequences {cn}n≥0⊂[0,c0]\{c_{n}\}_{n\geq 0}\subset[0,c_{0}] where 0≤c0<min⁡{2,2​a}0\leq c_{0}<\min\{2,2\sqrt{a}\}, {tn}n≥0⊂ℝ+\{t_{n}\}_{n\geq 0}\subset\mathbb{R}_{+} with tn→+∞t_{n}\to+\infty and {xn}n≥0⊂ℝN\{x_{n}\}_{n\geq 0}\subset\mathbb{R}^{N} with ∥xn∥≤cntn\lVert x_{n}\lVert\leq c_{n}t_{n}. Then, we consider the limit functions

limn→+∞F⁡(tn+t,xn+x)=F∞​(t,x),\lim_{n\to+\infty}F(t_{n}+t,x_{n}+x)=F_{\infty}(t,x),
limn→+∞C⁡(tn+t,xn+x)=C∞​(t,x),\lim_{n\to+\infty}C(t_{n}+t,x_{n}+x)=C_{\infty}(t,x),

which converge locally uniformly to (F∞,C∞,H∞)(F_{\infty},C_{\infty},H_{\infty}), an entire solution of the system

{∂tF∞=Δ​F∞+a​F∞​(1−C∞−F∞),∂tC∞=Δ​C∞+C∞​(1−C∞−F∞)+s⁡(F∞+C∞)​H∞,∂tH∞=d​Δ​H∞+b​H∞​(1−g​F∞−g​C∞−H∞).\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}F_{\infty}=\Delta F_{\infty}+aF_{\infty}(1-C_{\infty}-F_{\infty}),\\ &\partial_{t}C_{\infty}=\Delta C_{\infty}+C_{\infty}(1-C_{\infty}-F_{\infty})+s(F_{\infty}+C_{\infty})H_{\infty},\\ &\partial_{t}H_{\infty}=d\Delta H_{\infty}+bH_{\infty}(1-gF_{\infty}-gC_{\infty}-H_{\infty}).\end{aligned}\right.

Note that, the lower estimate (6.3) implies that (F∞+C∞)​(t,x)≥1(F_{\infty}+C_{\infty})(t,x)\geq 1 for all (t,x)∈ℝ×ℝN(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{N}.

{∂tH~∞=Δ​H~∞+b​H~∞​(1−g−H~∞),H~∞​(0,x)=H∞​(0,x).\left\{\begin{aligned} &\partial_{t}\widetilde{H}_{\infty}=\Delta\widetilde{H}_{\infty}+b\widetilde{H}_{\infty}(1-g-\widetilde{H}_{\infty}),\\ &\widetilde{H}_{\infty}(0,x)=H_{\infty}(0,x).\end{aligned}\right.

It is clear that, if g>1g>1, the function (t,x)→e−(g−1)​(t+t0)(t,x)\to e^{-(g-1)(t+t_{0})} is a super-solution of the above equation for any t>−t0t>-t_{0}. Since H∞​(−t0,x)≤1H_{\infty}(-t_{0},x)\leq 1 for any t0∈ℝ+t_{0}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}, it follows from the comparison principle that

H∞​(0,x)≤e−(g−1)​t0.H_{\infty}(0,x)\leq e^{-(g-1)t_{0}}.

By passing the limit as t0→+∞t_{0}\to+\infty, one gets that H∞≡0H_{\infty}\equiv 0. limn→+∞H⁡(tn,xn)=0,\lim_{n\to+\infty}H(t_{n},x_{n})=0,

which implies (6.1) holds true. If g=1g=1, one can consider the super-solution as 1/(b​t+b​t0+b)1/(bt+bt_{0}+b), for all −t0<t<+∞-t_{0}<t<+\infty where t0∈ℝ+t_{0}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}.

The statement (6.1) and the strong maximum principle implies that H∞≡0H_{\infty}\equiv 0. Then, by applying Claim 6.2 again, one can conclude that (F∞+C∞)≡1(F_{\infty}+C_{\infty})\equiv 1, which completes the proof of the statement (6.2). □\square

However, to investigate the profiles of solutions in the region of c∗⁣∗t≤∥x∥≤c0tc^{**}t\leq\lVert x\lVert\leq c^{0}t, one need to apply the uniform lower estimate of the F+CF+C-component in Theorem 2.4 and Theorem 2.5. Since the arguments for proving Theorem 2.8 and Theorem 2.9 are almost same, here we just show the proof of Theorem 2.8.

Proof of Theorem 2.8. 6.2 Asymptotic profiles in the low conversion rate case (g<1g<1)

The key point of studying the asymptotic profiles in the low conversion rate case is to provide a uniform lower estimate of the HH-component in the final zone. However, for the general case, it is hard to give the necessary and sufficient condition under which the HH-component is uniform positive from below. In this subsection, we first show two sufficient conditions for obtaining the uniform lower estimate of the HH-component. Then, we show that the CC-component and HH-component would converge to (C∗,H∗)(C^{*},H^{*}) as t→+∞t\to+\infty in the final zone.

The first sufficient condition means if conversion rate gg is small enough, then the population density of hunter-gatherers alway stay uniform positive.

{Ct=C⁡(1−C)+s​C​H,Ht=b​H​(1−H−g​C).\left\{\begin{aligned} &C_{t}=C(1-C)+sCH,\\ &H_{t}=bH(1-H-gC).\end{aligned}\right.

We expect the solution of the PDE system (1.1) to converge uniformly to the equilibrium (C∗,H∗)(C^{*},H^{*}) as t→+∞t\to+\infty.

Let us introduce the set Σ={(C,H)∈ℝ2: 0<C<1+s, 0<H<1}\Sigma=\{(C,H)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\ :\ 0<C<1+s,\ 0<H<1\}, in which (C∗,H∗)(C^{*},H^{*}) is the unique singular point. There exists a strictly convex function Φ:Σ→ℝ\Phi:\Sigma\to\mathbb{R} of class C2C^{2} that attains its minimum point at (C∗,H∗)(C^{*},H^{*}) and satisfies

(C⁡(1−C+s​H),b​H​(1−H−g​C))⋅∇Φ​(C,H)≤0​for all(C,H)∈Σ.(C(1-C+sH),bH(1-H-gC))\cdot\nabla\Phi(C,H)\leq 0\ \mbox{for all}\ \ (C,H)\in\Sigma.

The function Φ\Phi is a strict Lyapunov function in the sense that: if (C,H)(C,H) denotes the solution of corresponding Ode system (2.12) with the initial data (C0,H0)(C_{0},H_{0}), then

Φ⁡(C⁡(t),H⁡(t))=Φ⁡(C0,H0)​for allt>0⇒(C0,H0)=(C∗,H∗).\Phi(C(t),H(t))=\Phi(C_{0},H_{0})\ \mbox{for all}\ \ t>0\Rightarrow(C_{0},H_{0})=(C^{*},H^{*}).

As a matter of fact, we can consider the strictly convex functional as

Φ⁡(C,H):=b​g​∫C∗Cη−C∗η+s​∫H∗Hξ−H∗ξ.\Phi(C,H):=bg\int_{C^{*}}^{C}\frac{\eta-C^{*}}{\eta}+s\int_{H^{*}}^{H}\frac{\xi-H^{*}}{\xi}.

It is not difficult to check that, for all (C,H)∈Σ(C,H)\in\Sigma, it holds

(C⁡(1−C+s​H),b​H​(1−H−g​H))⋅∇Φ​(C,H)=−b​g​(C−C∗)2−b​s​(H−H∗)2≤0.(C(1-C+sH),bH(1-H-gH))\cdot\nabla\Phi(C,H)=-bg(C-C^{*})^{2}-bs(H-H^{*})^{2}\leq 0.

Furthermore, for any solution (C,H)(C,H) of the ODE system, one has

Φ​(C,H)t\displaystyle\Phi(C,H)_{t} =b​g​(C−C∗)​(1−C+s​H)+b​s​(H−H∗)​(1−H−g​H)\displaystyle=bg(C-C^{*})(1-C+sH)+bs(H-H^{*})(1-H-gH)
=−b​g​(C−C∗)2−b​s​(H−H∗)2,\displaystyle=-bg(C-C^{*})^{2}-bs(H-H^{*})^{2},

hence it is a strict Lyapunov function. Since Φ\Phi is bounded from below, we assume without loss of generality that Φ≥0\Phi\geq 0, and the equality only holds at the unique minimizer (C∗,H∗)(C^{*},H^{*}).

Let us argue by contradiction and assume that there exist c∈[ 0,c∗)c\in[\ 0,c^{*}) and a sequence {(tk,xk)}k≥0⊂(0,∞)×ℝN\{(t_{k},x_{k})\}_{k\geq 0}\subset(0,\infty)\times\mathbb{R}^{N} such that tk→+∞t_{k}\to+\infty and δ>0\delta>0 such that for all k>0k>0,

∥xk∥≤ctkand|C(tk,xk)−C∗|+|H(tk,xk)−H∗|≥δ.\lVert x_{k}\lVert\leq ct_{k}\ \ \mbox{and}\ \ |C(t_{k},x_{k})-C^{*}|+|H(t_{k},x_{k})-H^{*}|\geq\delta.

Consider the sequence of functions (Fk,Ck,Hk)​(t,x)=(F,C,H)​(t+tk,x+xk)(F_{k},C_{k},H_{k})(t,x)=(F,C,H)(t+t_{k},x+x_{k}). Now, let us fix c′>0c^{\prime}>0 such that c<c′<c∗c<c^{\prime}<c^{*}. Therefore, there exist N>0N>0 large enough and ε>0\varepsilon>0 small enough such that, for k≥0k\geq 0 and t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, one has

t+tk≥Aand∥x∥≤c′t+(c′−c)tk⇒{Fk​(t,x)≤1k,ε≤Ck​(t,x)≤1+s−ε,ε≤Hk​(t,x)≤1−ε.t+t_{k}\geq A\ \ \mbox{and}\ \ \lVert x\lVert\leq c^{\prime}t+(c^{\prime}-c)t_{k}\Rightarrow\left\{\begin{aligned} &F_{k}(t,x)\leq\frac{1}{k},\\ &\varepsilon\leq C_{k}(t,x)\leq 1+s-\varepsilon,\\ &\varepsilon\leq H_{k}(t,x)\leq 1-\varepsilon.\end{aligned}\right.

Then, by parabolic estimates, possibly along a subsequence, one may assume that

(Fk,Ck,Hk)​(t,x)→(F∞,C∞,H∞)​(t,x)locally uniformly for(t,x)∈ℝ×ℝN,(F_{k},C_{k},H_{k})(t,x)\to(F_{\infty},C_{\infty},H_{\infty})(t,x)\ \ \mbox{locally uniformly for}\ \ (t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{N},

sup(t,x)∈ℝ×ℝN​C∞​(t,x)<1+sandsup(t,x)∈ℝ×ℝ​H∞​(t,x)<1.\underset{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{N}}{\sup}C_{\infty}(t,x)<1+s\ \ \mbox{and}\ \ \underset{(t,x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}}{\sup}H_{\infty}(t,x)<1.

Moreover, it holds

|C∞​(0,0)−C∗|+|H∞​(0,0)−H∗|>0.|C_{\infty}(0,0)-C^{*}|+|H_{\infty}(0,0)-H^{*}|>0.

In order to reach a contradiction, we claim that

Let (U,V)(U,V) be a bounded entire solution satisfying the above estimates, then (U,V)​(t,x)≡(C∗,H∗)(U,V)(t,x)\equiv(C^{*},H^{*}).

≤\displaystyle\leq 0.\displaystyle 0.

and W∞W_{\infty} is a sub-solution of the heat equation, hence W∞​(t,x)≡W∞​(0,0)W_{\infty}(t,x)\equiv W_{\infty}(0,0) is a constant function. The strict convexity of Φ\Phi provide that
